title: Cloud Computing: An Introduction
topics: AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet.
Services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and AI.
It allows individuals and organizations to rent computing resources on demand.
Analogy: Paying for electricity consumed, not owning the power plant.
On-demand self-service: Users access resources without human interaction.
Broad network access: Services available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: Providers share resources across multiple customers securely.
Rapid elasticity: Resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: Usage is monitored and billed according to resources consumed.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Delivers fundamental computing resources like virtual machines, storage, and networking (e.g., AWS EC2).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): Provides infrastructure plus a development platform with built-in tools and databases (e.g., Google App Engine).
Software as a Service (SaaS): Delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet, accessed via a browser (e.g., Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom).
Public Cloud: Services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations, cost-effective.
Private Cloud: Dedicated to a single organization, offering more control and security.
Hybrid Cloud: Combines public and private clouds for balanced flexibility and security.
Community Cloud: Shared by several organizations with common goals or requirements.
Reduces costs by eliminating heavy investment in hardware and maintenance.
Improves scalability, allowing businesses to easily expand or reduce resources.
Enhances flexibility, enabling access to applications and data from anywhere.
Provides reliability through backup, disaster recovery, and high availability.
Supports innovation by allowing faster experimentation and deployment.
Security and privacy concerns due to data stored on remote servers.
Risk of downtime, as services depend on internet connectivity.
Compliance with strict industry regulations for data storage.
Vendor lock-in, making it difficult and costly to switch providers.
Performance concerns for applications requiring high speed or low latency.
Data storage and backup (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox).
Business collaboration tools (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams).
Entertainment streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix, Spotify).
Healthcare solutions like electronic medical records and telemedicine.
Education platforms for online courses and virtual classrooms (e.g., Coursera).
Research for large-scale data analysis, machine learning, and AI projects.
Cloud computing supports AI and big data analytics by providing high-performance resources.
Edge computing processes data closer to the source, relying on the cloud for management.
Multi-cloud strategies are gaining popularity to avoid vendor lock-in and improve reliability.
Serverless computing allows developers to focus on code, with infrastructure managed by the provider.
Future focus includes enhanced security, compliance, and integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G.
